lead: Garlic and paprika. The stew of the Albufera fishermen that rivals the Valencian paella in history and pedigree. Catarroja, El Palmar and the lake where it was born.

All i pebre is the most “from here” dish in all of Valencian cuisine. While paella can be made anywhere in the world with the right ingredients, all i pebre belongs to one specific territory: the Albufera, its fishermen, its irrigation channels, its eels. It is a dish of identity, memory and place. Powerful thanks to the garlic and paprika, and striking for its use of eel — an animal found at the mouths of the rivers of the Levante and in the Albufera lake — all i pebre is one of the most renowned stews in Valencian cooking.
A good all i pebre should not skimp on garlic, chilli, paprika or eel. And always, always, bread to mop up the broth. The lean, intense meat of the eel deserves to be sucked clean off the bone.

items.title: All i Pebre · Garlic and Paprika · The Rival of Paella
items.subtitle: Fishermen’s stew · Albufera de Valencia · The essence of the lake in a bowl
items.body: All i pebre — literally “garlic and paprika” in Valencian — is the great unknown dish of Valencian cuisine outside the Comunitat. While paella has conquered the world, all i pebre has remained the best-kept secret of the shores of the Albufera: the fishermen’s dish, the one shared by dipping bread into the red, spicy broth, drinking wine and chatting at dusk beside the lake. More than a recipe, it is a traditional cooking method for stewing fish with a powerful base of garlic, paprika and chilli. But in Valencia, when someone says “all i pebre” and nothing more, everybody knows what is meant: the eel of the Albufera, cooked slowly in an earthenware pot, with broken potatoes and a thick, reddish broth that demands bread and time.
facts: Albufera de Valencia · Catarroja and El Palmar · Earthenware-pot stew · A dish of farming and seafaring character

items.title: The Eel · The Star Ingredient
items.subtitle: Albufera eel · Rich, sweet meat · Oily fish of the Albufera
items.body: The eel is the fish of the Albufera par excellence. This long, slippery-skinned fish — which spawns in the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic and migrates to the Mediterranean — was for centuries the staple food of the fishermen of Catarroja and El Palmar. Its meat has notes that are sweet and intense at once, and a rich, firm texture that lets it absorb the garlic and paprika broth perfectly. The eel is cut into pieces three to five centimetres long, seasoned and added to the stew near the end of cooking, because its flesh cooks faster than the potato. Today the wild eel of the Albufera is increasingly scarce — the species is at conservation risk — and many restaurants turn to fish farms in the area. Outside El Palmar and Catarroja, finding it fresh at the market is difficult.
facts: Pieces of 3–5 cm · Added at the end of cooking · At conservation risk · Alternative: monkfish or mullet

items.title: The Mortar · The Technique of All i Pebre
items.subtitle: Crushed garlic · Chilli · Optional fried bread and almonds · Earthenware pot
items.body: The technique of all i pebre begins in the mortar. The garlic — in some versions a whole head is used in its skin, in others it is crushed — is worked together with the cayenne chilli until it forms a paste. This crushed base is the soul of the dish: powerful, aromatic, spicy. In an earthenware pot (preferably) or a tall casserole, the base is gently fried in olive oil — the garlic must not burn, as it would make the whole broth bitter —, the sweet paprika is added quickly and the pot is immediately topped up with water to stop it burning. The most orthodox version also includes fried bread and almonds crushed in the mortar, which thickens the broth naturally and rounds out the flavour. The potatoes are “chascadas” — they are broken rather than cut with a knife — so that the starch they release thickens the broth during the slow cooking.
facts: Mortar: garlic + chilli + (fried bread + almonds optional) · Earthenware pot · Slow cooking 45–60 min

items.title: Suc d’Anguila vs All i Pebre · The Difference Matters
items.subtitle: With potato = Suc d’Anguila · Without potato = pure All i Pebre · The purists know it
items.body: Among Valencian purists there is a clear debate: authentic all i pebre contains no potato. When potato is added to the stew, the dish becomes known as “suc d’anguila” (literally, eel broth), which differs in texture and in name, though it is still delicious. The only ingredients allowed in the traditional all i pebre competition of Catarroja are: oil, garlic, salt, potato, paprika, chilli, eel and water. The version without potato — pure all i pebre — has a thinner, more concentrated broth, in which the flavour of the garlic and paprika takes centre stage. The version with broken potatoes — the suc d’anguila — has a thicker, silkier broth, and the potato soaks up all the juices of the stew. In the restaurants of El Palmar and Catarroja, the version with potato is the most common and the one tourists know as “all i pebre”.
facts: Pure all i pebre: no potato · Suc d’anguila: with broken potato · Both versions in the competitions of Catarroja and El Palmar

items.title: Variations · Espardenyà, Cebollà and Beyond
items.subtitle: Espardenyà: with chicken and rabbit · Cebollà: with onion · Monkfish or mullet in all i pebre
items.body: All i pebre has generated a tree of variations that speak of its versatility. The espardenyà is the surf-and-turf version: a sofrito of chicken and rabbit (or duck) is added to the stew, creating a dish of extraordinary richness and depth. The cebollà replaces the potato with onion, with a sweeter, silkier result. The monkfish all i pebre — named by analogy — is the easiest version to find outside the Albufera: monkfish, thanks to its firm, chewy texture, withstands slow cooking perfectly and takes on the flavour of the sauce exceptionally well. There are also versions with mullet, octopus and cuttlefish. In Catarroja, the restaurants with the longest history — such as La Primitiva or Anguilas El Galet — have spent decades maintaining the most authentic versions. In Serra, the restaurant Casa Granero has won several national awards with its all i pebre.
facts: Espardenyà: + chicken and rabbit · Cebollà: + onion instead of potato · Monkfish all i pebre: the easiest alternative

items.title: The garlic must not burn
items.body: If the garlic browns too much, the broth turns bitter — a gentle, controlled sofrito

items.title: Paprika and water, quickly
items.body: Paprika burns in seconds — add water immediately after the sofrito

items.title: Broken potatoes
items.body: Break rather than cut — the starch that comes out thickens the broth naturally

items.title: Eel at the end
items.body: Eel cooks faster than potato — add it for the last 15–20 min of cooking

items.title: Slow heat
items.body: A gentle bubble, covered, 45–60 min — haste ruins this stew

items.title: Better the next day
items.body: The potatoes settle and the eel takes on all the aroma of the sauce as it rests

items.title: La Primitiva · Catarroja
items.body: One of the oldest restaurants on the Catarroja jetty. It began in the early 20th century as a tavern for port workers. Primitiva Cases was its first cook and founded an institution.
facts: Port of Catarroja · On the shores of the Albufera

items.title: Anguilas El Galet · Catarroja
items.body: A whole lifetime devoted to eel. Leonor Guillén made it a benchmark. They sell live eel and cook the all i pebre with patience, controlled heat and an earthenware pot.

items.title: Casa Baina · Catarroja
items.body: A classic of the port of Catarroja. The same menu as La Primitiva: authentic all i pebre with mullet salad and roasted peppers as a starter. Traditional cooking without frills.

items.title: Restaurants of El Palmar
items.body: The lakeside village of 700 inhabitants has more than thirty typical restaurants. Cañas y Barro, Ca Jaume, La Perleta, Llar del Pescador, El Redolí and Mornell are some of the leading names.
facts: El Palmar · 10 km south of Valencia

items.title: Casa Granero · Serra
items.body: A surprise: in the heart of the Sierra Calderona, this restaurant has won several national all i pebre awards. It shines just as much with a soupy rice as with the eel stew.

items.title: Catarroja and El Palmar Competition
items.body: Catarroja holds the oldest all i pebre competition. El Palmar also has its own “Concurs d’all i pebre tradicional de l’Illa d’El Palmar”, which brings together more than 2,500 people and 200 professionals.

blocks.title: What you should know about all i pebre
items: All i pebre with potato is technically called “suc d’anguila” among purists — although restaurants call it all i pebre anyway
The wild eel of the Albufera is increasingly scarce and expensive — many restaurants now use farmed eel from the area
If you cannot find eel, monkfish is the best alternative — its firm texture withstands slow cooking just as well
All i pebre is better the next day — the potatoes settle and the sauce gains depth as it rests
To eat it like the Albufera fishermen: village bread, red wine and no rush — the broth at the bottom is the reward
The Catarroja Competition and the El Palmar Concurs are the most authentic events for experiencing all i pebre first-hand
